segments.t: In Gabriel's office at ASK, Sofia Leprince shows him a video recording of a musical play. As they watch her performance together, Gabriel is deeply moved by her singing and acting talent. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Un prisonnier qui chante, c'est très original.
Ne faites pas attention à la robe.
Tu as raté quelque chose d'important.
Je reviens un peu en arrière.
Let's examine how Gabriel and Sofia share a tender moment watching her tape.
Un prisonnier qui chante, c'est très original.
'A singing prisoner, that is very original.' Gabriel notes the unusual tape, finishing with a clear cognate. In French, this is perfectly fine.
Ne faites pas attention à la robe.
'Do not pay attention to the dress.' Sofia is embarrassed, using a formal negative command meaning 'do not make attention'. A standard way to speak in French.
'It is a short film without money.' She explains the low budget with a handy chunk literally meaning 'without silver'. In French, you will hear this.
'Are you still his assistant?' Gabriel asks about her old job using the polite 'you', joined by a cognate. The French say this often.
'No, not anymore.' Sofia answers quietly with a handy chunk literally meaning 'more now'. In French, this is quite common.
'This passage is funny, look.' She points out a moment using a casual command to look. This is how you say it in French.
'Shall we do this later?' She suggests stopping, building from the everyday spoken 'we' and a handy chunk meaning 'later'. A handy phrase in French.
'No, let us continue, it is fine.' Gabriel insists on watching, using a group command to continue, plus 'it goes'. A useful expression in French.
Tu as raté quelque chose d'important.
'You missed something important.' Sofia points out his distraction with a past action meaning 'you missed'. This is very typical in French.
Je reviens un peu en arrière.
'I am going back a little.' She rewinds using an action meaning 'return', joined by a handy chunk meaning 'backwards'. A common chunk in French.
'We resume here, watch closely.' You'll hear the everyday 'we', followed by an action meaning 'take up again'. You will hear this in French.
'This passage is really good.' She highlights her acting with a handy sentence meaning 'this passage is well'. This is perfectly natural in French.
'Are you okay, Sofia?' Gabriel checks on her using a very common everyday expression that literally asks 'it goes'. In French, it works nicely.
'Yes, I am moved.' Sofia admits her feelings with a short response, changing the final sound because she is a female speaker. The French use this a lot.
'It is wonderful, Sofia.' Gabriel reassures her warmly by starting with 'it is' and a clear cognate. In French, it sounds perfect.

'You are really wonderful.' He shifts to the casual 'you' to express his sincere romantic admiration directly. This is standard in French. Now let's listen to the whole discussion again without stopping.
Un prisonnier qui chante, c'est très original.
Ne faites pas attention à la robe.
Tu as raté quelque chose d'important.
Je reviens un peu en arrière.
Gabriel has watched Sofia's performance tape and is captivated by her talent and charm. Their bond deepens as Sofia realizes Gabriel truly believes in her. See you next time!
